reviews.summary: The driving concept received an encouraging response [1]. One commenter suggested adding flying vehicles or animals [2], and also proposed alternate routes that change the other cars’ paths [3]. Those two feature suggestions come from the same person.

Readers welcomed the idea of making habit formation part of a game [1]. A concern was whether the game can encourage honest reporting of real-world tasks [2]. Another commenter proposed comparing habit outcomes between groups with and without the game [3]; that is a research suggestion, not evidence that the game changes habits.

A commenter requested an option to invert vertical controls [1]. Another questioned whether the displayed airspeed and turning behaviour match the plane’s motion [2]. A third expressed interest in playing [3]. The physics criticism is a source opinion, not a verified simulation test.

Two commenters thought the demonstration looked laggy [1][2]. One also questioned whether simulated players predict performance with real network connections [1]. The comments suggest a useful follow-up test with real clients; they do not establish a measured player limit.

One visitor reported being unable to start the game and then mentioned a Cloudflare error in a second comment [1][2]. These are two messages from one person, describing an access problem on October 6 rather than evidence that the game is currently unavailable.

One commenter liked the ticking sound effect [1] and suggested retaining an option to choose older sound effects [2]. The same person proposed wall-mounted armour recharge stations or small supply rooms [3]. These are specific sound and level-design suggestions, without an explicit report of having played.

The cat-racing premise prompted playful suggestions: yarn balls and hairball hazards [1], plus a mode where robot vacuums ignore their riders [2]. A separate presentation suggestion was to remove the black header box [3]. These are proposed additions, not confirmed features.

One player reported a softlock within the first thirty seconds after destroying a rock before a tree [1]. That sequence is a concrete reproduction lead for the opening tutorial. Another commenter encouraged continued development [2]. The report has not been independently reproduced here.

The eyes-closed concept drew praise [1]. Suggestions included blacking out the display instead of dimming it [2] and penalising repeated eye opening to discourage progress through constant blinking [3]. Another commenter worried that parallax makes movement distance harder to judge [4].

Two commenters suggested building the trailer from actual gameplay footage [1][2]. Another felt the store capsule promised a cosy experience that did not match the gameplay screenshots [3]. The actionable theme is consistency between the marketing preview and what players can expect to see in the game.

A commenter found the game interesting but suggested choosing between running and boarding, and criticised the camera’s angles [1]. Another left a brief positive reaction [2]. The first response is mixed feedback with concrete control and camera concerns.

One commenter wanted clearer visual and sound feedback for hits, stronger gun effects, and changes to the dash and perceived damage [1]. Another suggested making elemental impacts more visible through effects such as shattering or exploding enemies [2]. Neither comment explicitly confirms hands-on play.

The tank-game preview received praise for its explosions [1] and lighting [2]. Another commenter liked the sound and animations [3], while a fourth said the game looked appealing enough to try [4]. These reactions describe presentation and interest, not measured gameplay satisfaction.
